Farhan caught me at the lift, quietly, like he was handing over a parcel. “People are saying you got the senior role because you're close to the director, and that you and Meera from finance are together.” I laughed it off, but by afternoon I could feel it: the pantry going quiet, eyes sliding away. I'm Nitin, by the way.

For two weeks I arrived at eight, wore my sharpest shirt and never left before the director did, just so nobody could say I was slacking. I stopped talking to Meera altogether. It was exhausting. I spent more energy on what they thought than on my actual work. One evening Sanjay, who never gossips, said, “You look tired, man. Are you okay?” And I nearly cried.

I'm Sarika, and I sit behind Jagdish on the accounts floor. Last month the talk started. Why does he leave at five sharp on Thursdays? Is there someone? Did the promotion come from a friend upstairs? Nobody said it to his face, but he heard. I saw his shoulders change.

The next week Jagdish came in at eight, stopped leaving at five and straightened his tie whenever the manager walked by. He skipped lunch invitations so nobody could ask questions. I can't say what he was feeling. He looked like someone on a stage. Pooja from payroll, who had started half of it, kept glancing at him and then at her screen. I nearly told her to stop, but I didn't. I'm still not sure Jagdish knows I noticed.

Charu had been promoted to team lead at the Hyderabad office on Monday. By Wednesday, Rajni pulled her into the stairwell. “Don't be upset. But people in the pantry are saying you got it because you and Mr Verma have lunch together. And they're asking why you're still not married at twenty-six.”
Charu felt her face burn. She had lunch with Mr Verma twice, both times with the whole team.
That week she stopped going to lunch at all. She changed her shirt twice before leaving home. She wrote every email three times, checking whether it sounded too friendly. She even took the long route to her desk so she wouldn't pass his cabin.
By Friday she was exhausted, and she hadn't done any of the work she'd been promoted for.

qa.q: How many times had Charu had lunch with Mr Verma?
qa.a: Twice, both times with the whole team.

qa.q: How did Charu feel when Rajni told her what people were saying?
qa.a: She felt exposed and humiliated, her face burning at the speculation about her promotion and personal life.

qa.q: What could Charu do instead of managing her image all week?
qa.a: She could focus on her work, keep her normal routine, and if needed calmly raise the gossip with her manager or HR.

qa.q: How might Rajni have felt telling Charu?
qa.a: Rajni was probably uneasy and caring, wanting Charu to know even though it would hurt.

“Lalremsiami, can I tell you something?” Simran whispered at the coffee machine. “People think you're pregnant. Because you keep leaving early on Thursdays.”
“What? I have physiotherapy for my back!”
“I know that. But you know how they are. Somebody said you're hiding it before appraisals.”
Lalremsiami stared at her cup. “Great. So now what?”
The next Thursday, she stayed till seven and moved her physio to Saturday. On Monday she wore a tight kurta on purpose. In the team meeting she mentioned her “bad back” three times.
Simran leaned over. “You're trying very hard.”
“I'm trying to make them stop.”
“They don't even remember,” Simran said gently. “You're the only one still thinking about it.”

qa.q: Why does Lalremsiami leave early on Thursdays?
qa.a: She has physiotherapy for her back.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami feel when Simran told her what people thought?
qa.a: She felt exposed and frustrated at being speculated about, and started worrying about how she looked to others.

qa.q: What went wrong in how Lalremsiami responded, and what might work better?
qa.a: She changed her schedule and clothes to control the talk; it would be easier to keep her physio and let the rumour fade, or speak to HR if it continues.

qa.q: How does Simran see Lalremsiami's efforts?
qa.a: Simran sees she's trying too hard and gently points out that others have already forgotten.

I'm Abhinav, and last year I spent two months managing a rumour that wasn't even true.
I'd taken four Fridays off, one each week, to take my father for physiotherapy after his fall. I didn't tell anyone why. Raghav, from the next desk, finally said, “Bro, the whole floor thinks you're interviewing with the competitor.”
Suddenly I was performing loyalty. I posted about how much I loved the company. I stayed late on Thursdays so nobody would think I was slacking. I laughed extra loud at my manager's jokes. Every time I walked into the pantry and conversation stopped, my chest tightened.
Then my manager asked me straight, and I told her about my father. She said, “Why didn't you just say?” It was over in a minute.

qa.q: Why had Abhinav taken four Fridays off?
qa.a: To take the father for physiotherapy after a fall.

qa.q: How did Abhinav feel walking into the pantry during those months?
qa.a: Abhinav felt exposed and anxious, chest tightening whenever conversation stopped.

qa.q: What finally ended the rumour, and what does that suggest?
qa.a: The manager asked directly and Abhinav explained; a short, honest word early might have saved two months of image-managing.

qa.q: How might Raghav have felt telling Abhinav about the rumour?
qa.a: Raghav was probably concerned and a bit awkward, wanting to warn a colleague.

Team lead's note, follow-up with Dolma.
Since Dolma's promotion to senior analyst was announced, I've heard the pantry version: that she got it because she is "close to the director", plus questions about why she still isn't married. Alka told me Dolma overheard some of it on Tuesday.
Since then, Dolma copies me on every email, even two-line replies. She stayed till nine twice this week redoing slides that were already fine. At lunch she sits with a different group each day, as if checking who is on her side. In our meeting she said, "I just want them to see I earned it," and then apologised three times for taking my time.
What I did next: I told Dolma plainly that the promotion was based on her project results, and put that in writing. I asked her to stop copying me on routine mail. At Friday's team meeting I said that colleagues' personal lives are not team business.

qa.q: How many times did Dolma stay till nine this week?
qa.a: Twice this week.

qa.q: What does Dolma copying the lead on every email suggest?
qa.a: Dolma feels exposed and anxious, trying to prove she earned the role and to control how others see her.

qa.q: How could the lead's steps help Dolma stop spending energy on her image?
qa.a: A written reason for the promotion and a public line against personal talk take away what she was trying to defend, so she can just work.

qa.q: What would change for Dolma if the team stopped the speculation?
qa.a: She could stop redoing finished slides and testing lunch tables, and put that energy back into her actual job.
